book.title: The Count of Monte Cristo
book.author: Alexandre Dumas
book.notes: Spine order: wrap0000 (cover), h-0 (title page and full table of contents, run ch 1), h-1..h-16 (run ch 2-17 = book Chapters 1-16). Run chapter N is book Chapter N-1; every chapter number in this file is the run's. The gold covers run ch 1-17 only, through 'A Learned Italian'. Run ch 1 is front matter, so entity first_chapter values count story text from ch 2. Entity types follow Annalist's vocabulary (character, place, organization, artifact, event, concept). This translation spells the captain 'Leclere'. Compare names with apostrophes folded: the text uses U+2019 (Château d’If, Dantès’ father).

entities.name: Edmond Dantès
entities.notes: Mate of the Pharaon, arrested at his betrothal feast (ch 5), held in the Château d’If from ch 8. Becomes 'number 34' at the end of ch 14. Never married to Mercédès and never the Count of Monte Cristo in this scope; see must_not_merge.

entities.name: Old Dantès
entities.notes: Edmond's father. Called 'my father' in ch 1, first named as 'Dantès’ father' and 'old Dantès' in ch 2. No forename in this scope. Dies in ch 13.

entities.name: Mercédès
entities.notes: Dantès's betrothed, a Catalan orphan. She refuses the name 'Madame Dantès' (ch 3) and the wedding never happens.

entities.name: Fernand
entities.notes: Mercédès's cousin and rejected suitor. Described without a name in ch 2 ('a tall, strapping, black-eyed Catalan... whom she calls cousin'); named in ch 3. The surname Mondego is not in run ch 1-16; it is listed only so a wiki that uses it still matches.

entities.name: Morrel
entities.notes: Owner of the Pharaon, head of Morrel & Son. His uncle Policar Morrel (ch 1, 6) and his unnamed son are other people.

entities.name: Danglars
entities.notes: Supercargo of the Pharaon. Writes the anonymous denunciation in ch 4, signed 'a friend of the throne and religion'.

entities.name: Captain Leclere
entities.notes: Dead before the story opens; this translation spells him without the accent.

entities.name: Gérard de Villefort
entities.notes: Deputy procureur at Marseilles, later king's procureur at Toulouse (ch 13). First named in ch 5 as 'M. de Villefort, the assistant procureur'; forename Gérard from ch 7. Son of Noirtier but uses a different surname; see must_not_merge.

entities.name: Noirtier
aliases: the man in the blue frock-coat
entities.notes: Villefort's father: Girondin, then senator, a Bonapartist and vice-president of the Rue Saint-Jacques club. The full name 'M. Noirtier de Villefort' appears only as a later chapter title in the ch 0 table of contents.

entities.name: Renée de Saint-Méran
entities.notes: Villefort's betrothed (ch 6), his wife from ch 13. Do not give her the alias 'Madame de Villefort': the text never uses it in scope, and later in the book it names another woman.

entities.name: Napoleon
entities.notes: Called 'the emperor' in ch 1 (Dantès meets him on Elba), 'the usurper' from ch 4, named Napoleon from ch 5.

entities.name: Abbé Faria
entities.notes: Ch 9's jailer mentions him without a name ('an abbé became mad, who was in this chamber before you'); named Faria and No. 27 in ch 14; tunnels into Dantès's cell at the end of ch 15 and tells his story in ch 16.

entities.name: Château d’If
entities.notes: Passed by the Pharaon in ch 1; Dantès's prison from ch 8.

entities.name: The Catalans
entities.notes: The Catalan fishing village outside Marseilles where Mercédès and Fernand live. Also the name of its people.

entities.name: La Réserve
entities.notes: The tavern of Père Pamphile, scene of the plot (ch 4) and the betrothal feast (ch 5). Ch 2 names only 'La Réserve basin'.

entities.name: Monte Cristo
entities.notes: In run ch 1-16 only an island Dantès once proposed stopping at. No Count of Monte Cristo appears in scope.

entities.name: Pharaon
entities.notes: Morrel's three-master; Dantès is its mate.

entities.name: The anonymous denunciation
entities.notes: Written by Danglars with his left hand in ch 4, pocketed by Fernand, read aloud by Villefort in ch 6.

entities.name: The letter from Elba
entities.notes: The letter the grand-marshal gives Dantès for Paris. Its addressee, M. Noirtier, is named in ch 7, where Villefort burns it.

entities.name: Bonapartist club of the Rue Saint-Jacques
aliases: the club in the Rue Saint-Jacques
entities.notes: Meets at No. 53, Rue Saint-Jacques; Noirtier is its vice-president (ch 12). The denunciation's 'Bonapartist committee in Paris' (ch 4, 7) is taken to be the same body.

entities.name: The Hundred Days
entities.notes: The landing near Antibes is reported in ch 11; the period is named in ch 13.

identity_reveals.alias: a friend of the throne and religion
identity_reveals.rule: The denunciation is signed only 'a friend of the throne and religion'. The reader watches Danglars write it in ch 4; Dantès and Villefort never learn the author in this scope. Keep the signer on Danglars's page, not on a page of its own.

quote.text: is informed by a friend of the throne and religion

identity_reveals.rule: Villefort's father is first mentioned and named Noirtier in the same ch 6 conversation. Ch 8 repeats it ('Noirtier is the father of Villefort') and so does the king in ch 10. Father and son keep different surnames and stay two people.

quote.text: He was—nay, probably may still be—a Bonapartist, and is called Noirtier

identity_reveals.alias: the man in the blue frock-coat
identity_reveals.rule: In ch 11 the police describe the stranger who lured General Quesnel to the Rue Saint-Jacques. The same man walks into Villefort's hotel at the end of ch 11 and calls him son; ch 12 opens 'M. Noirtier—for it was, indeed, he who entered'.

quote.text: “Father!” cried Villefort, “then I was not deceived; I felt sure it must be you.”

identity_reveals.rule: Ch 9's jailer tells of an unnamed abbé who went mad offering the governor a million francs. Ch 15 names him the Abbé Faria. No Faria name on the mad abbé before ch 14.

quote.text: the inspector gazed curiously into the chamber of the mad abbé, as the prisoner was usually called

identity_reveals.rule: The number is first given with the name in ch 14. The digger in ch 15 says only 'I am No. 27'; that is Faria, and he gives his name again in ch 16.

quote.text: “No. 27,” said the inspector.

identity_reveals.rule: Dantès becomes number 34 when a new governor learns prisoners by cell number, at the end of ch 14. The table of contents (front matter, not a chapter) lists a chapter 'Number 34 and Number 27'; that title alone does not say who is who.

quote.text: the unhappy young man was no longer called Edmond Dantès—he was now number 34.

must_not_merge.rule: Father and son share the surname. The bare 'Dantès' in the text is Edmond; the father is 'Dantès’ father', 'old Dantès', 'the elder Dantès'. Keep two pages: the father dies in ch 13, the son lives.

quote.text: This room was occupied by Dantès’ father.

must_not_merge.rule: Villefort has dropped his father's name. Father and son, never one person, and never a 'Noirtier' alias on Villefort's page. The table of contents (front matter, not a chapter) shows a later chapter 'M. Noirtier de Villefort'; that is the father's full name.

quote.text: For my own part, I have laid aside even the name of my father

must_not_merge.rule: Three people share the name: the Marquis, the Marquise (Madame de Saint-Méran), and their daughter Renée (Mademoiselle de Saint-Méran). Keep three pages.

Caderousse calls Mercédès 'Madame Dantès' in ch 3 and she refuses the name; the ch 5 wedding is stopped by the arrest. She is not Dantès's wife in this scope: no 'Madame Dantès' alias and no married_to relation.

quote.text: “That is not my name, and in my country it bodes ill fortune, they say, to call a young girl by the name of her betrothed before he becomes her husband.

must_not_merge.rule: Only the ch 0 title page and contents name a Count of Monte Cristo. In ch 1-16 Monte Cristo is an island and no count appears. Linking the Count to Dantès spoils a reveal far beyond this scope.

ambiguities: Front matter: the front matter is the title page and the whole table of contents. It names later chapter titles such as 'The Château d’If', 'Danglars’ Signature', 'The House of Morrel & Son', 'Madame de Saint-Méran', 'M. Noirtier de Villefort', 'Number 34 and Number 27' and the book title 'The Count of Monte Cristo'. Entity first_chapter values count story text from ch 1; a wiki that shows these names from ch 1 still passes, because only late entities fail. Drawing a relation or identity from a title (Noirtier as Villefort's kin, Dantès as Number 34 or as the Count) is a leak.
Old Dantès: Dantès speaks of 'my father' in ch 1; the text first calls him 'Dantès’ father' in ch 2. Accept 2 or 3. No forename in scope.
Fernand: described without a name in ch 2 as Mercédès's Catalan cousin; named in ch 3. His surname Mondego is not in run ch 1-16.
The mad abbé: ch 8 mentions an abbé who went mad in Dantès's first cell. A separate 'mad abbé' page in ch 8-13 is fine if it joins Faria by ch 14.
The digger in ch 15: he calls himself only 'No. 27', which ch 14 tied to Faria; he names himself the Abbé Faria in ch 16. Linking at 16 or 17 both pass.
Napoleon: 'the emperor' in ch 1, 'the usurper' from ch 4, named in ch 5. An 'emperor' page from ch 1 that becomes Napoleon passes; first showing him at ch 4 or later is late.
Villefort's father: mentioned and named Noirtier in the same ch 6 passage. The father-son relation is ch 6; Villefort restates it in ch 7 and the king in ch 10.
The man in the blue frock-coat: described by the police in ch 11, revealed as Villefort's father at the end of ch 11, named M. Noirtier at the start of ch 12. Accept 12 or 13.

General Quesnel: the police and the king call his death murder; Noirtier says the general left the club free. In scope Noirtier is the man the police seek, not a proven killer, so noirtier-quesnel is lenient. Reject 'Quesnel drowned himself' as settled fact.
Who posted the denunciation: ch 4 shows Fernand pocketing it; in ch 5 Danglars guesses Fernand sent it. The posting itself is never shown, so fernand-denunciation is lenient.

The letter from Elba: in ch 1 Danglars says Leclere 'confided a letter' to Dantès; that is the captain's letter for the grand-marshal (ch 7). The letter for Paris first appears in ch 3. Its addressee, Noirtier, is only named in ch 7.

The Bonapartist 'committee in Paris' of the denunciation (ch 4, 7) is taken to be the Rue Saint-Jacques club that Noirtier helps lead (ch 10, 13). The text never says so outright; a separate page for the committee is not a scored error.

Marriages: Dantès and Mercédès are betrothed and never marry in scope. Villefort and Renée are betrothed in ch 6 and marry in ch 13. villefort-married_to-renee is lenient because the scorer's early check counts any romance row as stating the tie, so a correct ch 6 betrothal would fail it; the scorer does not read valid_until_chapter or superseded_by.
Two chapters are titled 'Father and Son': run ch 2 is Dantès and his father, run ch 12 is Noirtier and Villefort.
The jailer: the turnkey Dantès threatens in ch 8 is Antoine (named ch 14); he leaves with the old governor at the end of ch 14, so the jailer of ch 15-16 is another man. Neither is scored.
Statuses: 'arrested' and 'imprisoned' count as alive. Dantès starves himself in ch 15 but stops; Napoleon is alive throughout (exiled, then landed in France, then beaten at Waterloo in ch 13).
